note: Establish a six-column direct sequence selling the five blends and rejecting ethane; this gives a broad revenue baseline before tuning.
notebook:

Step 1: initial six-column baseline. Blends sacrifice only 15% and avoid many expensive close separations. Ethane must be rejected to make C3 saleable. Heavies initially left unsold. Settings moderate to limit energy/capital in expensive scenario.

note: Correcting every cut to the intended blend boundaries and adding ethane rejection plus the C3/C4 splitter. Higher root boil-up should move the distillate cut from C5 back to C4.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a six-column blend plant: root C4-/C5+, ethane removal, C3/C4 split, C5/C6+ split, C6-paraffin/naph+ split, and naph/heavy split. Tune flow splits via reflux versus boil-up, then reduce costs and recover heavies if worthwhile.
Step 2: Correct baseline cuts. Initial root 50/4/4 cut within C5 (T=1171 vs desired 864), so increase boil-up to 6. New T and TT columns reject ethane and split C3/C4. Other reboil/reflux ratios target component group flow ratios. Blend revenue ceiling about $2.49bn/yr, so avoiding pure-component polishing is attractive in this expensive scenario. Other agents' roots failed at 2.5/2.5; retain robust higher-duty settings initially.

note: Use measured flow trends to correct all major cuts: much lower root boil-up for C4-/C5+, then targeted C5, C6, naphthene and heavy-product splits.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a blend-focused plant: root C4-/C5+, ethane removal, C3/C4 split, C5/C6+ split, C6-paraffin/naph+ split, naph/heavy split, then heptane and octane/nonane recovery. Tune flow splits first, then purity and cost.
Step 3: Flow extrapolation from root runs gives boil-up about 2.2 for the desired 864 mol/s C4- tops (not 6). Keep the successful C3/C4 split but lower TT boil-up to reject only ethane. Set B and BB for 695 C5 tops and 1246 C6 tops respectively. Add a paraffin/naphthene splitter and simplify heavies to two columns. Revenue ceiling is about $2.5bn/yr; achieving sellable streams is the immediate priority.

note: Replace the failed tree with a known-converged skeleton and target three sellable light blends first. The C3/C4 split is sharpened while the root and C5 cuts are moved toward their component-flow targets.
notebook: PLAN: First establish a valid, revenue-positive core selling C3, C4 and C5 blends; then add and tune the C6-paraffin recovery branch, and only afterwards consider heavy products. Step 1 now: copy the known-converged four-column skeleton, raise the root cut to include C4, sharpen C3/C4, strip ethane, and lower the B boil-up to make a C5 tops cut. The failed 50/4/2.2 root is abandoned. R136 shows 50/5/2 converges; higher boil-up moves the cut upward. R136 also shows B boil-up 4 greatly overheads C5 feed, so 2.2 is a first correction. Defer BB because its 4/4 split was neither paraffin- nor naphthene-pure.

note: Build a low-cost valid light-products core: keep the converged root, sharpen propane/C4 separation, and add ethane stripping while removing the expensive unsaleable heavy branch.
notebook: PLAN: Establish a valid revenue-positive light-products core (C4 and C3 blends, ethane rejected), then add a C5 recovery branch only after measured cuts justify it. Current step: use R183's converged 50/5/2 root, increase the light-column boil-up to drive propane out of the C4 bottoms, and strip ethane from the C3 tops. Sell the entire heavy branch for now to avoid its very large cost. R183 showed 50/5/2 root converges and T60/6/4 gives C4 only 76% because 20% propane remains; higher boil-up should correct this. Its TT is C3 with 14% ethane, so a small third column should make a saleable C3 blend. Defer C5/C6 because B60/6/6 cost $305M/yr and its tops were only 53% C5.

note: Reduce all three column costs and pressure while increasing the C3/C4 split boil-up; this tests whether the two light blends can become profitable without the heavy branch.
notebook: PLAN: Establish a valid revenue-positive light-products core (C4 and C3 blends, ethane rejected), then add a C5 recovery branch only after measured cuts justify it. Current step: sharply reduce capital/refrigeration cost with shorter columns and larger pressure drops, while raising the C3/C4 column boil-up to remove propane from C4. Previous 50/5/2 root alone cost $168.5M/yr and left much C4 in bottoms; 60/8/6 T left C4 only 84% because of propane. TT is cheap ($8.4M/yr) and makes a saleable C3 blend. Target total cost below ~$140M/yr with C3+C4 revenue near $150M/yr. Defer C5/C6 because earlier B60/6/6 cost $305M/yr and its tops were only 53% C5.

note: Use the proven C5/C4 blend core, remove the costly heavy branch, and test whether lower pressure makes the three-column sequence profitable.
notebook: PLAN: Adopt the demonstrated C5+C4 blend sequence, discard the unprofitable heavy branch, and reduce pressure/refrigeration cost; then tune the light split and add only clearly profitable recovery. Step 1: copy R274's successful root/T/TT cuts, sell B, and test dp=0.3 throughout. R274 earned $566M/yr C5 plus $157M/yr C4; without its B/BT columns those revenues should cover root+T+TT costs if pressure reduction works. Its root 50/4/6 cleanly puts C5 in T; T 60/8/12 makes TB 95% C5; TT makes TTB a C4 blend. My own low-pressure root was much cheaper, so this is the best route to a positive baseline. Avoid pure-product polishing and C6 columns until this core is profitable.

note: Restore R324's profitable low-pressure core and increase only the inexpensive C3 finishing column so its 90%-C3 bottoms should exceed blend specification.
notebook: PLAN: Revert to R324's proven dp=0.1 four-column core, then monetize its nearly qualified C3 bottoms before trying lower-cost light splits. Step 1: copy R324 and sharpen only the very cheap ethane-rejection column. Its TTTB is 90% C3 mix (71% propane +19% propylene), so modestly higher stages/reflux/boil-up should cross 95% and unlock roughly $70M/yr for little extra cost. Keep root/T/TT unchanged to preserve $736.5M/yr revenue and the 0.297 baseline. My dp=0.3 experiment destroyed both blend purities and greatly raised costs; do not revisit high pressure drop. Heavy C6 branches from R323/R326 cost $500M+/yr without sales and remain unattractive.

note: Test a substantially sharper, hotter C3 finishing split: expel the residual isobutane from TTTB while preserving enough C3 to exceed the 95% blend threshold.
notebook: PLAN: First finish the inexpensive C3 recovery test on the current clean-TT core; if it fails, copy R370's 0.329 three-column design and optimize its costly stages. Step 1: raise only TTT severity (60 stages, R=8, boil-up=6). At boil-up 2 and 3 its bottoms stayed 90% C3 because about 24 mol/s isobutane remained; a stronger reboil should expel isobutane while extra stages/reflux limit propane loss. Root/T/TT remain unchanged, preserving C5 and C4 sales. R370 is the fallback: 50/5/5 TT saves $17M/yr and avoids the useless TTT column, though its C4 revenue is $13M/yr lower. Heavy C6 branches cost more than their added sales. Avoid dp=0.3 and root/T reflux reductions, which destroyed blend purity.

note: Adopt the best three-column core and reduce only the C3/C4 splitter, whose bottoms already have essentially complete C4 purity.
notebook: PLAN: Adopt R418's best 0.379 three-column core, then spend remaining solves on low-risk cost reductions while preserving both blend specifications. Step 1: test TT at 40 stages, R=4, boil-up=4; its current C4 bottoms have essentially zero non-C4 material, so some separation margin can be traded for lower cost. Root and T are unchanged. If purity falls, revert toward 50/5/4. R417 shows that trimming T to 50/7 costs more revenue than it saves. Heavy branches remain uneconomic; prior high-severity C3 finishing did not reach sale spec.

note: Adopt the best 0.382 core and make a small, isolated reduction in root stages; unchanged reflux and boil-up should retain both blend cuts.
notebook: PLAN: Start from R470 (0.382), reduce root cost incrementally while preserving its fixed feed split, then tune the C4/C5 column if worthwhile. Step 1: copy R470 and test root 45 stages at unchanged R=4, boil-up=6. R467's failure changed both root severity and T together, so it does not rule out a modest stage-only reduction. Root is $306.5M/yr, over half total cost. TT=50/5/4 is essential; reducing it loses C4 blend value. Heavy branches and C3 polishing have so far been uneconomic.

note: Test heat integration on the dominant root column while preserving the proven split and both downstream blend columns. The large pressure difference should make the HP condenser hotter than the LP reboiler.
notebook: PLAN: Start from the best R518 three-column core (0.383) and attack the dominant $306.5M/yr root energy cost. If heat integration fails or costs rise, revert and use remaining solves for modest single-column energy reductions. Root stage cuts save almost nothing; T boil-up 10 destroys C5 sales and T=50 loses more revenue than it saves. Heavy branches and C3 polishing have so far been uneconomic.

note: Revert the failed double effect and make only a modest root boil-up reduction, targeting its dominant reboiler duty while preserving the sharp C5/C6 cut.

Current step: test root boil-up 5.7 while holding R=4 and 50 stages; check whether the C5 blend stays >=95%.

TT reflux 4.0 lost $11M revenue for $3M savings.

notebook: PLAN: Adopt the validated R709 four-column core now, then use remaining solves only for isolated tuning of its cheap ethane stripper or C3/C4 splitter.
